title: Insert a Node at a Specific Position in a Linked List
directAnswer: Walk exactly position − 1 nodes to land on the node that will sit just before the new one, then do the two-line splice: newNode.next = prev.next; prev.next = newNode. Position 0 is the special case — there is no predecessor, so you insert at the head and return the new head. Everything else is O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.pattern: Walk to predecessor, then splice (set new.next before rewiring prev.next)
remember.formula:
if position == 0: newNode.next = head; return newNode
prev = head
repeat position - 1 times: prev = prev.next
newNode.next = prev.next
prev.next = newNode
return head
rules: To insert *at* index `k`, stop on the node at index `k − 1` — walk `position − 1` steps, not `position`.
Set `newNode.next = prev.next` **before** `prev.next = newNode`. Reverse the order and you lose the rest of the list.
Position `0` has no predecessor — insert at the head and **return the new head**, don't try to walk.
The head can change, so the function must **return the (possibly new) head**, never assume the caller keeps the old one.
Use a counter loop, not a `while (cur.next != null)` loop — you're stopping at a fixed index, not the end.
whenToUse: Insert into a singly linked list at a known 0-based index
Building or editing a list where order matters and you have the target slot
Any 'splice one node between two existing nodes' subproblem
Warm-up for harder relink problems (reverse a sublist, rotate, reorder)
antiSignals: You always insert at the front → that's O(1) insert-at-head, no walk needed
You always insert at the back and keep a tail pointer → O(1) append, no walk
Random access by index is needed repeatedly → an array or dynamic array beats a linked list
The structure is a doubly linked list with a known node reference → splice in O(1) using prev/next directly
remember.takeaway: Every linked-list insertion is the same two-line splice — the only question is how you reach the predecessor. Get the walk-to-position-minus-one and the set-next-before-rewire ordering right and rotate, reorder, and reverse-sublist all become routine.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can manipulate next pointers without losing the tail, count to the right predecessor (position − 1), and handle insertion at the head as a distinct case that changes the returned head.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Walking position steps instead of position − 1, or writing prev.next = newNode before newNode.next = prev.next and orphaning the rest of the list.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Call out the two invariants up front: stop one node early, and wire the new node's next before touching the predecessor's next. Mention that position 0 returns a new head, which is why the function returns a head at all.

problemStatement:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list, an integer `data`, and an integer `position` (0-based).

Insert a **new node** holding `data` so that it ends up at index `position` in the list. Return *the head of the modified list*.

You may assume `0 ≤ position ≤ length`, so inserting at `position == length` appends to the end.
constraints: The list is singly linked (next pointers only)
understanding: We splice a brand-new node into the chain at a given 0-based slot. To put a node *at* index k, we must first reach the node at index k − 1 (its predecessor) and rewire two links. Index 0 has no predecessor, so it becomes the new head.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is position 0-based or 1-based?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 0-based. Inserting at position 0 makes the new node the head; position == length appends at the tail.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is position guaranteed to be within [0, length]?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That means I never walk off the end, but I still treat position 0 (new head) as a separate branch.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the list be empty?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — an empty list with position 0 just returns the new node as the only element.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I allocate a new node or move an existing one?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Allocate a new node holding data. We're inserting, not relocating, so a single new node is created.

examples.explanation: Walk position − 1 = 0 steps → stop on node 1. Splice 9 between node 1 and node 2.
Position 0 has no predecessor: newNode.next = head, return newNode as the new head.
position == length appends: walk to the last node (index 2), its next is null, splice 9 after it.

approaches.name: Iterative — Walk to Predecessor, Then Splice (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. It's the canonical answer and the building block for every harder relink problem.
hints: To slip a node into index k, which existing node do you actually need a handle on — the one at k, or the one just before it?
Reaching index k − 1 means taking k − 1 steps from the head. What happens when k is 0 and there is no node before it?

Once you're standing on the predecessor, you need two links: the new node must point to what came after the predecessor, and the predecessor must point to the new node. Order those two assignments carefully.
approaches.complexityReasoning: We take at most position − 1 ≤ n − 1 steps to reach the predecessor, then do O(1) pointer work. No extra structures, so O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
We reach the node directly before the target slot, then rewire two pointers to drop the new node in.

**Why the predecessor, not the target.** In a singly linked list you can only attach a node by editing some existing node's `next`. To put a node *at* index `k`, the node whose `next` must change is the one at index `k − 1`. So the whole job is: get a handle on the predecessor, then splice. That's why we walk `position − 1` steps, not `position`.

**Why position 0 is special.** Index 0 has no predecessor — there's no node whose `next` we can edit. Instead the new node becomes the head: point its `next` at the old head and return it. This is exactly why the function returns a head at all: only here does the head change, and the caller has to learn about it.

**The two-line splice, and why order matters.** Standing on `prev`, we do `newNode.next = prev.next` first, then `prev.next = newNode`. The first line saves the rest of the list onto the new node; the second hooks the new node into place. Flip them and `prev.next = newNode` overwrites the only reference to the tail before you've copied it — `prev.next` now points at `newNode`, and `newNode.next = prev.next` just points the new node back at itself. The tail is gone. **Set the new node's next before you touch the predecessor's next.**

**Why the loop is counted, not condition-driven.** We aren't walking to the end of the list; we're walking to a fixed index. A `for` loop that runs `position − 1` times lands precisely on the predecessor. A `while (cur.next != null)` loop would overshoot to the tail.
approaches.insight: The named trap here is losing the next pointer. The instant you overwrite `prev.next` you've discarded your only link to everything downstream — so you stash it on `newNode.next` first. That 'save the next pointer before you rewire' reflex is the single most reused move across reverse, rotate, and reorder.

dryRun.intro: position is 1, so we walk position − 1 = 0 steps and stay on the head (node 1), the predecessor.

java.explanation: No predecessor exists at index 0 — handle it as a head insert.
Point the new node at the current head before returning it.
Walk position − 1 steps to land on the predecessor, not the target slot.
Save the rest of the list onto the new node BEFORE rewiring — this is the lost-next trap.
Now hook the new node into place after the predecessor.
Head is unchanged for any position > 0, so return the original head.

python.explanation: Index 0 has no node before it; insert at the head.
New node points at the old head, which it now precedes.
Counted walk of position − 1 steps stops exactly on the predecessor.
Stash the downstream list first so we don't lose it.
Link the predecessor to the freshly inserted node.

pitfalls: Walking position steps instead of position − 1 — you overshoot and insert one slot too late.
Writing prev.next = newNode before newNode.next = prev.next — orphans the entire tail.
Forgetting the position == 0 branch — a null predecessor causes a crash or a dropped head.
Not returning the head — the caller silently keeps the old head and loses a head insert.

edgeCases.behavior: Empty list, head insert: newNode.next = null, return newNode → [5].
position == length: walk to last node (index 2), prev.next is null, splice 9 at the tail → [1, 2, 3, 9].
Single node, append: prev stays on node 7, newNode.next = null, prev.next = newNode → [7, 4].

approaches.name: Recursive — Decrement Position Down the List
approaches.whenToMention: Mention as a clean alternative that frames insertion as a smaller subproblem; flag the O(n) call-stack cost versus the iterative O(1).
hints: If inserting at position p in the whole list, what is the equivalent problem on head.next?
Each step that doesn't insert moves one node forward and reduces the target position by one.
The base case is position == 0: build the new node, point it at the current head, and return it as the new sub-head.
approaches.complexityReasoning: One recursive call per node walked, up to position ≤ n calls, each O(1) → O(n) time. The recursion depth equals position, so O(n) stack space in the worst case.
approaches.explanation:
We express insertion as: insert at position p in `head` equals attach `head` in front of (insert at position p − 1 in `head.next`).

**The base case carries the splice.** When `position == 0`, the new node belongs right here: set `newNode.next = head` and return `newNode`. Every caller above takes that returned sub-head and reattaches it as its own `next`, so the splice ripples back up the chain automatically.

**The recursive step rebuilds the prefix.** For `position > 0`, the current head stays where it is; we recurse on `head.next` with `position − 1` and assign the result to `head.next`. Reassigning `head.next` is what stitches the (possibly new) sub-head back in — it's the same 'attach the merge of the rest' shape used in list recursion generally.

**Why the iterative version is the safer lead.** This reads cleanly and needs no explicit predecessor handling, but each node walked adds a stack frame. With n up to 1000 that's fine here, yet on long lists the iterative O(1)-space walk avoids any stack-overflow risk. Same O(n) time, more space — so present iterative first and offer this as the elegant variant.
approaches.insight: Recursion hides the predecessor bookkeeping inside the call stack: 'reassign head.next to the recursive result' is the splice, performed implicitly as calls unwind. It's the same move as recursive merge — attach the current head in front of the solved remainder.

dryRun.intro: Each call peels one node and decrements position until it hits 0, where the new node is built.

code.python:
def insertNodeAtPosition(self, head: ListNode, data: int, position: int) -> ListNode:
    if position == 0:
        new_node = ListNode(data)
        new_node.next = head
        return new_node
    head.next = self.insertNodeAtPosition(head.next, data, position - 1)
    return head

java.explanation: Base case: the new node belongs at this exact spot.
New node points at the current sub-head, which it now precedes.
Recurse on the rest with one fewer step, then reattach the returned sub-head.
This node is unchanged as a head for position > 0.

python.explanation: Insert right here when the countdown reaches zero.
Splice: new node leads, old sub-head follows.
Reassigning head.next stitches the recursive result back in.

pitfalls: Missing the position == 0 base case — infinite recursion or a null dereference on head.next.
Forgetting to reassign head.next to the recursive result — the splice never connects.
Using recursion on very long lists where the iterative O(1)-space walk is safer.

commonMistakes: Walking position nodes instead of position − 1 and inserting one slot too far.
Overwriting prev.next before saving prev.next onto the new node — the tail is lost.
Not treating position 0 as a head insert, then dereferencing a null predecessor.
Forgetting to return the head, so a changed head never reaches the caller.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Rewiring in the wrong order (losing the next pointer)
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Setting prev.next = newNode first overwrites the only reference to the rest of the list. The follow-up newNode.next = prev.next then points the new node at itself, and every downstream node is orphaned.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
prev.next = newNode;
newNode.next = prev.next;  // prev.next is now newNode — points to itself!
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
newNode.next = prev.next;  // save the tail first
prev.next = newNode;       // then hook in

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Off-by-one on the walk
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Inserting at index k requires standing on index k − 1. Walking k steps lands on index k, so the new node ends up one slot too late.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
prev = head
for _ in range(position):   # one step too many
    prev = prev.next

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ignoring the head-insert case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Position 0 has no predecessor. Walking position − 1 = −1 steps either skips the loop and leaves prev on the head (inserting at index 1, wrong) or dereferences null. Branch on it explicitly and return the new head.

followupVariations.title: Insert at Head
followupVariations.hint: The position == 0 case in isolation — O(1), no walk, just point the new node at the head and return it.

followupVariations.title: Delete a Node at a Position
followupVariations.hint: Same walk-to-predecessor, but relink prev.next = prev.next.next instead of splicing in.

followupVariations.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
followupVariations.hint: Reach a position relative to the tail with a two-pointer gap, then do the same predecessor relink.

patternNote: Walk-to-predecessor then two-line splice — the atomic move behind every linked-list edit. The same skeleton (reach a node, save its next, rewire) powers delete-at-position, reverse-a-sublist, rotate-list, and reorder-list.
